content: 1. The Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine and the yellow fever vaccine should not be administered to children with symptomatic HIV infection or AIDS. However, other vaccines can be safely given to these children. 2. The second or third dose of the DPT (Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus) vaccine should not be given to a child who has experienced convulsions or shock within three days of receiving the most recent dose. 3. The DPT vaccine should not be administered to children with recurrent convulsions or an active central nervous system disease. 4. If a child with diarrhea is due to receive the oral polio vaccine, the vaccine should still be administered. However, this dose should not be counted as part of the regular immunization schedule. A note should be made in the child’s immunization record indicating that the dose was given during an episode of diarrhea, so an additional dose can be provided later. 5. If the child has a health card, this information should be recorded on it, and the mother should be advised to show the card to the health worker during future visits. If no health card is available, the details should be written in a short note for the mother and health worker. 6. In countries where yellow fever poses a risk, the yellow fever vaccine should be included in the immunization schedule. In exceptional situations where measles morbidity and mortality in infants under nine months of age account for more than 15% of cases and deaths, an extra dose of the measles vaccine should be given at six months of age. The scheduled dose should still be administered as soon as possible after the child reaches nine months of age. 7. An additional measles vaccine dose is also recommended for high-risk groups, such as infants in refugee camps, hospitalized infants, HIV-positive infants, and those affected by disasters or during measles outbreaks. A second opportunity to receive a measles vaccine dose should be provided to all children. 8. Mothers taking their children home after hospital assessment should be advised on when to return to a health worker for follow-up care. It is crucial to teach mothers the warning signs that indicate the need for immediate hospital return, such as inability to drink or breastfeed, worsening illness, fever, recurrence of illness after treatment, fast or difficult breathing, blood in stool, or poor drinking during diarrhea. 9. For children with feeding problems, follow-up should occur within five days to assess whether recommended feeding changes have been implemented and to provide further counseling if needed. For children with anemia, follow-up should occur in 14 days to administer additional oral iron. Children with very low weight require additional follow-up in 30 days, including weighing, reassessment of feeding practices, and further nutritional counseling. 10. Practical procedures, such as administering injections or inserting intravenous cannulas, should be explained to parents or the child (if old enough) beforehand, including any associated risks. Consent should be obtained. Procedures on young infants should be performed in warm surroundings to prevent hypothermia, and good lighting is essential. Older children should be informed about what to expect, and analgesia should be provided when necessary. 11. When administering injections, disposable needles and syringes should be used, and the injection site should be cleaned with an antiseptic solution. The name and amount of the drug administered should always be recorded. 12. Intramuscular injections in children over two years old should be given in the outer thigh or the upper, outer quadrant of the buttock, avoiding the sciatic nerve. For younger or severely malnourished children, the outer side of the thigh or the deltoid muscle in the upper arm is preferred. 13. Subcutaneous injections should be given at a 45° angle into the subcutaneous fatty tissue, avoiding the underlying muscle. The plunger should be drawn back to check for blood before administering the drug. 14. Intravenous cannulation should be performed with sterile equipment, and the site should be cleaned with an antiseptic solution. Peripheral veins, such as the cephalic vein in the antecubital fossa or the dorsal hand veins, are commonly used in children over two months old. Scalp veins may be used in children under two years old. The cannula should be secured with tape, and the site should be monitored for signs of infection or complications. 15. In emergencies where venous access is not possible, intraosseous infusion is a safe and reliable method for administering fluids and drugs. The proximal tibia is the preferred site for needle insertion, avoiding the epiphyseal plate. The needle should be advanced slowly until a sudden decrease in resistance is felt, indicating entry into the bone marrow cavity. 16. Central vein cannulation, such as the external jugular or femoral vein, should only be performed when intravenous access is urgently needed. The procedure should be conducted aseptically, and the cannula should be securely fixed in place. The site should be closely monitored for complications. 17. Umbilical vein catheterization can be performed in neonates within the first few days of life for resuscitation or exchange transfusion. The umbilical cord should be cleaned with an antiseptic solution, and the catheter should be advanced into the umbilical vein, ensuring it is not kinked and blood can be easily drawn back. 18. Nasogastric tube insertion involves measuring the distance from the nose to the earlobe and then to the xiphisternum. The tube should be lubricated and passed through one nostril into the stomach. Proper placement should be confirmed by aspirating stomach contents and checking the pH. 19. The child should be positioned appropriately, and the procedure should be conducted aseptically. The site should be prepared with an antiseptic solution, and local anesthesia may be used for older, alert children.
